Hey guys, I understand the dissatisfaction relating to my decision in donation system and I would like to apologize.

It was never my intention to generate some kind of profit for this project, I genuinely wanted to help a new community grow. Because of public opinion, I have removed all possible ways to donate without contacting me directly.

For those of you who have accused me of not understanding the ELUA, I would like to clear something up. In short, the ELUA states that you cannot give rewards for donating that the player cannot get without donating. This means OP perks such as /god, /heal, /repair, etc. Items and claimblocks however are obtainable legitimately, which is why I decided to use them as rewards for donators. I was very careful not to breach the ELUA, however I am a man of the people and I will do what the majority wants.

I sincerely apologize for this.

I've been playing for a little bit on the server and I have a few observations/recommendations, if you're willing to hear them. I used to admin a fairly large public survival server, for whatever that's worth.

Things I like:

  • I think you've done a great job with spawn - I especially like the tutorial area, and the signs indicating how far out spawn protection extends

  • the message players get when leaving spawn

  • The colored VoatMC branding in automated messages - that's quite clever and really makes it stand out.

  • grief prevention! It's very convenient and noob-friendly, so kudos on selecting it!

  • the trade room is kind of neat!

  • protection from monsters while inside spawn is interesting, could be handy for deterring mob-based spawn-killing

  • crafting recipes for horse armor (though I might like it if they were slightly more expensive)

  • that /me is enabled

  • the rules and /rules

  • edit: the afk notification is nice.

  • The amount of effort you have put into all of this - even in some of the things that I dislike it's apparent that you care about making the server nice.

Things I dislike

  • The rank tags in chat, eg.

<| Voater | Mumberthrax>

  • Lockette. Signs spamming up chests is annoying to look at, is somewhat redundant with grief prevention already protecting chests inside claims.

  • Trade area being a random floating island not inside spawn protected region

  • xp as currency in the server shop. XP is too easy to grind and acquire, nullifying the challenge and fun of playing.

  • command-based teleports being easy/free (/tpa, /spawn)

  • pvp being disabled

  • starting with a full inventory of tools

  • crafting recipes for nametags - these are already renewable via fishing, and a crafting recipe cheapens them. I'm ok with the saddle one though because horses should be used.

Things I'm more or less neutral on

  • quickshop. I think the idea of player run shops is nice (better than admin-run shops), though I've not messed with this particular shop plugin.

Recommendations

  • The following plugins: https://voat.co/v/VoatCraft/comments/252880/872036

  • remove lockette. Consider LWC as an alternative - without auto-locking.

  • enable pvp outside of spawn, trading areas. alternatively use a plugin that lets people toggle off whether they want to pvp or not. eg http://dev.bukkit.org/bukkit-plugins/pvptoggle/

  • remove the enchanting table and anvils at spawn so that acquiring these things for oneself - at least at the initial phase of the map - is a challenge

  • remove the starting tool/supply set. Instead put a small public melon farm and a small automated tree farm at spawn. (like with this http://dev.bukkit.org/bukkit-plugins/worldguard-treefarm-flag/)

  • As mentioned in the plugin list, PLEASE consider getting a block-logging plugin like prism, coreprotect, or logblock.

  • Configure grief prevention to make trees fall when they are chopped. It's such a handy thing for players, and it prevents floating tree spam.

  • a /help command for players that gives some basic information about the server, and the most commonly used commands

  • have no ranks for players. If you must have a tag for global chat, make it unobtrusive.

  • move the trade/shop area to be inside the spawn protected region, either on the ground, floating above spawn, or belowground.

  • If you're going to use quickshop, design the shop area around that. Let players run the economy and give them a venue in which to do it.

  • host some events for players to compete in, with prizes being some rare of valuable items, as well as a reasonable amount of claim blocks for grief prevention.

  • if enabling pvp, consider using http://dev.bukkit.org/bukkit-plugins/pwnpvpbalance/

  • if enabling pvp, then enable siege mode in grief prevention configs

  • set some kind of cooldown on teleports

  • be professional and do not give mod positions to people for donating, don't abuse admin/mod powers.

  • edit: pre-generate the map out to a certain distance using the worldborder plugin, so players don't cause lag by exploring

  • edit: consider turning off NocheatPlus's chat spam limiter in favor of GriefPrevention's, since NCP can be overly agressive if not tuned properly

Some more radical suggestions

  • Consider trying out extra hard mode: http://dev.bukkit.org/bukkit-plugins/fun-hard-mode/ - especially for the ender dragon respawning. It's very compatible with grief prevention

  • Consider trying out mineralvein http://dev.bukkit.org/bukkit-plugins/mineral-veins/

  • Consider using nerdspawn https://github.com/NerdNu/NerdSpawn and selecting a handful of respawn areas around the map

  • edit: consider using CobraCorral for horse locking - and for finding your lost horses. https://github.com/TheAcademician/CobraCorral/

  • edit: even crazier suggestion is to use Citadel in addition to grief prevention - for larger or community projects. it isn't super noob-friendly, but then noobs probably wouldn't be using it much anyway. grief prevention would be enough for their needs generally speaking.

That's all I have for now! I'm sure I'll come up with more but this is probably enough for the time being to make this server really stand out.

I'll typically determine if I like something based on the first episode no matter the length of the series. I don't really drop anime for failing to hook me anymore, and I like slow paced anime. If I drop something either of the following should be true (with a few exceptions):

a) The narrative in the show doesn't interest me. For example, I dropped Arslan Senki because I'm not really interested in shonen action shows (regardless of how good they are).

b) I perceive the show as bad. For example, I thought Plastic Memories had a pretty awful first episode, so not going to continue watching that because the show becoming good after that is highly unlikely.

But it can vary greatly depending on the type of story you want to tell, although as a rule of thumb spending at least one episode introducing the characters and the world before moving on to the plot is a good idea. It helps you get invested in the characters, and therefore you will care about what is going on when the plot starts moving. And if you're going to go on for long (say 4+ episodes) then there generally needs to be something else than introduction going on. Like a mystery hook or characterization. You know, anything but the characters doing random things just in order for you to get attached to them.

2-3 Episodes, which seems to be the consensus here. I watched a lot of Eureka Seven because it came on between two other anime I liked, so I ended up watching it by proxy. Characters seem a little...formulaic. I gave Black Lagoon and Deathnote three episodes before I decided they just weren't for me, though it was a stretch to watch that many of Deathnote. Usually after that much you can tell if an anime is going to be to your liking or not.

The best pacing is what works best for that story. Attempting to quantify the "proper" length and pacing of the beginning of a story, without any regard for the story itself, is closer to Mad Libs than storytelling. The sombre, unhurried beginning of Graveyard of the Fireflies shouldn't be shortened or sped up just because Pom Poko was half an hour longer and had a more rousing beginning.

I keep watching a show as long as it keeps being worth my time. The show might turn out to be garbage by the second or seventh or even first episode—whether I stick around for the whole trip is generally up to the quality of the screenplay.

I generally follow the rule of 3, but with a few variants:

  1. Episode 1 has to not suck. It can be kinda boring, it can be a little cliche, the plot can be unexplained, but so long as it's not bad I'll wait to see if it gets good. In other terms, there has to be a net-positive appeal. This season's episode-1 drop was Prison School; an odd setting, uninspired jokes, and an ecchi component that relies on the viewer finding BDSM sexy. Three strikes, out.
  2. Episode 2 has to have some distinctive entertainment. By now there has to have been one point in the show that I can point to and say "This was funny/exciting/sad/dramatic, and the show is going to have more of it." This season's passing marks were Monster Musume's opening scene and the "Ice Cream Incident," GATE's wholesale slaughter of 150,000 soldiers, and Shimoneta's... everything.
  3. Episode 3 is the cutoff for the episode 2 mark if the show's a little slow or building up.

My general rule is 3 episodes, but I've watched more and watched less before dropping in different circumstances. For me though, there needs to be some sort of hook within those first three episodes. A good example for me would be Gunslinger Stratos. I actually gave that show 4 episodes before dropping. Because the concept intrigued me, then the slow burn to build the story killed it. Typically though 3 episodes should give you a decent idea of if you're going to like a show or not, with very few exceptions.

I usually watch an anime until it starts to feel like a chore. If an anime can't get me hooked until I reach this point then I probably wouldn't enjoy the rest of it and I'll drop it. This is a good rule for even not bad anime. If watching it starts to feel like a chore, even if it's good, put it on hold. I did this with One Piece. I fucking love that anime but watching it started to feel like a chore and I'd start to feel a bit stressed if I didn't watch a lot. So I put it on hold as soon as I got too the time skip.

To be honest it differs from anime-to-anime. Some shows I can tell on the first episode that I'm going to hate it. Other shows will spark a bit of interest and I'll decide to give them a few episodes (usually 3-5) before I decide whether to drop them or not.

I'm hard to please in terms of anime I watch, if it can't make me interested with the first episode I drop it. I don't like to waste any time watching something I'll probably not enjoy. And if it's just especially boring or lame, I may not even finish the first episode. If it CAN pique my interest in the first episode, I'll usually give it another episode or two before I decide to continue or drop.

I watch an anime series I pick up all the way to the end. I like watching things to the end, never dropping an anime except when the anime I've viewed is just plain baaad..
